a: he reaped a hundred times what he sowed
p: The same Hebrew letters can be read "measures" or "barley." The Greek reads "barley."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: a hundred measures
readings.plain: he reaped a hundred times what he sowed

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: barley yielding a hundredfold
readings.plain: he reaped barley, a hundred times what he sowed

why: The consonants are the same; only the vowels differ. The Hebrew vowel tradition reads she'arim, "measures," a word found only here in this sense. The Greek translators read se'orim, "barley," which suits the dry Negev, where barley grew better than wheat. Both are old, and the meaning hardly changes. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew tradition.

p: The Greek has "We did not find water." The Hebrew words for "to him" and "not" sound the same.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Samaritan Pentateuch; Targums; Vulgate
readings.en: and they said to him, "We have found water"
readings.plain: "We have found water."

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.orig: καὶ εἶπαν Οὐχ εὕρομεν ὕδωρ (reading לֹא, lo', "not")
readings.en: and they said, "We did not find water"
readings.plain: "We did not find water."

why: In Hebrew lo ("to him") and lo' ("not") sound alike, and the Greek translators read the second. Their reading makes Isaac name the dry well "Oath" (the Greek gives Horkos) after the oath just sworn, not after water. The Hebrew reading fits the story of wells found and named in this chapter, and it is followed by all other witnesses.

a: is like the smell of a field
t: A field, or a full field?
p: The Samaritan and Greek texts read "a full field."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: like the smell of a field
readings.plain: is like the smell of a field

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: like the smell of a full field
readings.plain: is like the smell of a full field

why: The extra word may be an old reading lost from the Hebrew, or a translator's and scribe's way of making the picture richer. The sense is the same: a field rich with the LORD's blessing. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: And Esau raised his voice and wept.
p: The Greek adds that Isaac was deeply troubled before Esau cried aloud.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: and Esau lifted up his voice and wept
readings.plain: And Esau raised his voice and wept.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.orig: κατανυχθέντος δὲ Ισαακ ἀνεβόησεν φωνῇ Ησαυ καὶ ἔκλαυσεν
readings.en: and as Isaac was stung to the heart, Esau cried out with a loud voice and wept
readings.plain: Isaac was deeply moved, and Esau raised his voice and wept.

why: The Hebrew is shorter, and the Greek phrase looks like an addition that softens Isaac by showing his pity. Translators generally prefer a shorter reading when the longer one can be explained as an addition. The Greek is a witness to how early readers felt the scene.

p: The written Hebrew has one word, "With fortune!"; the reading tradition has two, "Fortune has come!"

readings.w: Masoretic Text, read form (Qere); Targums; KJV "A troop cometh"
readings.en: fortune has come
readings.plain: Good fortune has come!

readings.w: Masoretic Text, written form (Ketiv); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC) (Ἐν τύχῃ)
readings.en: with fortune! / how fortunate!
readings.plain: With good fortune!

why: This is a Ketiv/Qere: the scribes copied the letters as written but marked how to read them aloud. The written form, begad, means "with luck!" or "luckily!"; the Greek "In fortune" agrees with it. The reading tradition splits it into two words, "fortune has come." The meaning is almost the same. The Plain English Translation follows the read form, as most translations do.

a: while Jacob tended what was left of Laban's flock.
t: The Samaritan text adds Jacob's dream here
p: The Samaritan Pentateuch inserts the dream that Jacob later reports in 31:11–13, so that it happens in its place.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: and Jacob was tending the rest of Laban's flock
readings.plain: while Jacob tended what was left of Laban's flock.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC); partly preserved in the Reworked Pentateuch scroll from Qumran, 4Q364 (first century BC)
readings.orig: ויאמר מלאך האלהים אל יעקב בחלום ...
readings.en: adds the angel's speech of 31:11–13
readings.plain: while Jacob tended what was left of Laban's flock. Then the angel of God said to Jacob in a dream, "Jacob." He said, "Here I am." He said, "Look up and see: all the male goats mounting the flock are streaked, speckled and mottled, because I have seen everything Laban is doing to you. I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a standing stone and made a vow to me. Now get up, leave this land, and go back to the land of your birth."

why: In 31:11–13 Jacob tells his wives about a dream the story never showed. The Samaritan Pentateuch, which often fills such gaps, adds the dream at the point where it would have happened, in nearly the same words as Jacob's later report (the added text above is given in this translation's wording of 31:11–13). Emanuel Tov uses this passage as a standard example of Samaritan harmonizing, and notes that the Reworked Pentateuch scroll 4Q364 shares the expansion, so it predates the Samaritan community's own text. The shorter Hebrew is almost certainly older: the story lets Jacob reveal the dream himself. The Plain English Translation follows it.

a: I am the God of Bethel
t: "The God of Bethel" or "the God who appeared to you"?
p: The Hebrew grammar here is unusual. The Greek and an Aramaic translation expand it.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: I am the God (of) Bethel
readings.plain: I am the God of Bethel

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC); compare Targum Onqelos
readings.orig: ἐγώ εἰμι ὁ θεὸς ὁ ὀφθείς σοι ἐν τόπῳ θεοῦ
readings.en: I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God
readings.plain: I am the God who appeared to you at Bethel

why: In Hebrew "the God" (ha'el) with the article before a place name is awkward, and some scholars think words such as "who appeared to you" fell out (compare 35:1). The Greek has that longer text, and Targum Onqelos similarly explains "who revealed myself to you at Bethel." But the longer reading may also be a smoothing of the hard Hebrew. The meaning is the same either way: the God of Jacob's vow (28:18–22).

a: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, may they judge between us, the God of their father.
p: The Hebrew verb is plural. The Samaritan and Greek have a singular verb, and the Greek lacks the last phrase.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.orig: אֱלֹהֵי אַבְרָהָם וֵאלֹהֵי נָחוֹר יִשְׁפְּטוּ בֵינֵינוּ אֱלֹהֵי אֲבִיהֶם
readings.en: may they judge between us, the God of their father
readings.plain: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, may they judge between us, the God of their father.

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC)
readings.en: may he judge between us
readings.plain: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, may he judge between us, the God of their father.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.orig: ὁ θεὸς Αβρααμ καὶ ὁ θεὸς Ναχωρ κρινεῖ ἀνὰ μέσον ἡμῶν
readings.en: will judge between us (no last phrase)
readings.plain: The God of Abraham and the God of Nahor will judge between us.

why: The plural verb lets Laban call on two family gods, and the phrase "the God of their father" may be a scribe's note tying both to Terah. Scribes and translators who wanted one God made the verb singular, and the Greek drops the phrase (or its Hebrew text lacked it). The harder plural is more likely original. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

a: Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem
p: One Hebrew word, shalem, read as "safe" or as the town Salem.

readings.w: Masoretic Text as read by Jewish tradition (Rashi, Targums); most modern versions
readings.en: Jacob came safe to the city of Shechem
readings.plain: Jacob came safely to the city of Shechem

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC); Latin Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: καὶ ἦλθεν Ιακωβ εἰς Σαλημ πόλιν Σικιμων
readings.en: Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites
readings.plain: Jacob came to Shalem, a city of Shechem

why: The letters are the same; the question is whether shalem is an adjective or a name. "Safe, whole" fits Jacob's vow to return "in peace" (28:21) and the Hebrew word order. The KJV and the ancient translations took it as a town, and a village called Salim lies near Nablus. Both are possible; the Plain English Translation follows the Jewish reading tradition.

a: God had revealed himself to him
p: The Hebrew verb with "God" is plural; the Samaritan, Greek and Latin make it singular.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: God (or the heavenly beings) revealed themselves to him
readings.plain: God had revealed himself to him

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC); Vulgate
readings.en: God revealed himself to him
readings.plain: God had revealed himself to him

why: English cannot show the difference without forcing a meaning, so the Plain English Translation wording is the same either way. The plural is the harder reading, and the same thing happens at 20:13, where the Samaritan text also changes it to singular. Scribes tended to remove plural verbs with Elohim, not add them. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; see the note on this verse for what the plural may mean.

a: Then they set out from Bethel.
t: The Greek order of verses 16 and 21
p: The Septuagint opens this verse with the camp beyond the tower of Gader, which the Hebrew gives in verse 21.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC)
readings.en: Then they set out from Bethel
readings.plain: Then they set out from Bethel.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.orig: ἀπάρας δὲ Ιακωβ ἐκ Βαιθηλ ἔπηξεν τὴν σκηνὴν αὐτοῦ ἐπέκεινα τοῦ πύργου Γαδερ
readings.en: Jacob set out from Bethel and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Gader
readings.plain: Then Jacob set out from Bethel and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Gader.

why: The Greek moves the stop at Migdal-eder before Rachel's death, perhaps so that the journey reads in order: Bethel, the tower, then the road to Ephrath. It also turns the obscure kivrat into a place name, Chabratha. The Hebrew order, with the tower after the burial near Bethlehem, fits a tower of the flock near Bethlehem (compare Micah 4:8). The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew.

p: The Greek adds "and it seemed evil in his eyes." The Hebrew has a gap here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (with a blank space in mid-verse); Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: and Israel heard
readings.plain: and Israel heard.

readings.w: Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.orig: καὶ ἤκουσεν Ισραηλ καὶ πονηρὸν ἐφάνη ἐναντίον αὐτοῦ
readings.en: and Israel heard, and it appeared evil before him
readings.plain: and Israel heard, and it seemed evil in his eyes.

why: The Hebrew stops short: Israel heard, and then a space is left in the middle of the verse (a pisqa), as if the scribes marked a silence. The Greek fills the gap with Jacob's reaction. The added words are probably an explanation, so the Plain English Translation keeps the shorter Hebrew. Jacob's real response comes only on his deathbed (49:3–4).

a: daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite
p: Was Anah Zibeon's daughter or his son? 36:24 says Anah was Zibeon's son.

readings.w: Masoretic Text
readings.en: daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon
readings.plain: daughter of Anah, daughter of Zibeon the Hivite

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch; Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: daughter of Anah, son of Zibeon
readings.plain: daughter of Anah son of Zibeon the Hivite

why: In 36:24 Anah is a son of Zibeon, so "son of Zibeon" is easier, and many scholars think it original (the NRSV follows it). But the Masoretic "daughter of Zibeon" can mean that Oholibamah was Zibeon's granddaughter, as Hebrew "daughter" can mean any female descendant, and it appears again in 36:14. The easier reading may be a correction. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and lets "daughter of Zibeon" mean granddaughter.
b: The same verse calls Zibeon a Hivite, while 36:20 makes him a Horite. Many scholars suspect the very similar Hebrew letters were confused (חוי / חרי).

p: In 28:9 Ishmael's daughter is Mahalath. The Samaritan text reads Mahalath here and in 36:4, 10, 13 and 17.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: Basemath daughter of Ishmael
readings.plain: Basemath daughter of Ishmael

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC)
readings.en: Mahalath daughter of Ishmael
readings.plain: Mahalath daughter of Ishmael

why: The Samaritan Pentateuch makes chapter 36 agree with 28:9 everywhere the name appears, the kind of harmonizing it does often. That is exactly why the Hebrew, which leaves the difference standing, is likely older. The same choice applies in 36:4, 10, 13 and 17. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew; the ch. 36 page discusses the wives' names.

a: he went to a land away from Jacob his brother
p: The Hebrew names no land. The Samaritan and Greek read "from the land of Canaan"; the Syriac "to the land of Seir."

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: he went to a land away from Jacob his brother
readings.plain: he went to a land away from Jacob his brother

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch (medieval manuscripts of a text going back to the last centuries BC); Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: he went from the land of Canaan, away from Jacob his brother
readings.plain: he went away from the land of Canaan, from Jacob his brother

readings.w: Peshitta (Syriac translation, about AD 100–200)
readings.en: he went to the land of Seir
readings.plain: he went to the land of Seir, away from Jacob his brother

readings.w: Targum Onqelos (Aramaic, about AD 100–300)
readings.en: he went to another land
readings.plain: he went to another land, away from Jacob his brother

why: "He went to a land" with no name is awkward, and every ancient version smooths it in its own way, which suggests they all had the short Hebrew in front of them. A name such as Seir may have dropped out early, but no Hebrew manuscript has it. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and lets the next verses (36:8) name Seir.

p: Korah is a son of Oholibamah (36:5, 18). The Samaritan text does not list him here.

readings.w: Masoretic Text; Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Torah made in the 200s BC)
readings.en: chief Korah, chief Gatam
readings.plain: Chief Korah, Chief Gatam

readings.w: Samaritan Pentateuch
readings.en: chief Gatam
readings.plain: Chief Gatam

why: Korah is not among Eliphaz's sons in 36:11, and he appears again as Oholibamah's son in 36:18, so his name here may have been copied in by mistake from 36:18. The Samaritan reading avoids the problem and matches 36:11 and 1 Chronicles 1:36. But the harder Masoretic reading is supported by the Greek, and a clan of Korah could have been counted with Eliphaz's territory. The Plain English Translation follows the Masoretic Text and notes the difference.

a: These are the sons of Dishon
p: The Hebrew vowels here read Dishan, but the list and 1 Chronicles 1:41 show Dishon is meant.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Dishan
readings.plain: These are the sons of Dishan

readings.w: 1 Chronicles 1:41; the context (36:25); most translations
readings.en: Dishon
readings.plain: These are the sons of Dishon

why: This translation follows the consonants of the Leningrad Codex, and departs from it only when its own context shows a slip, saying so here. At 36:39 "Hadar" and "Hadad" are different letters and both are possible, so the Plain English Translation keeps Hadar. Here the difference is only a vowel letter, and the sons listed belong to Dishon son of Anah (36:25), not to Dishan, whose sons follow in 36:28. So the Plain English Translation prints Dishon.

p: The Leningrad Codex has Hadar; 1 Chronicles 1:50 and other witnesses have Hadad.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex)
readings.en: Hadar
readings.plain: Hadar

readings.w: Many Hebrew manuscripts; Samaritan Pentateuch; 1 Chronicles 1:50
readings.en: Hadad
readings.plain: Hadad

why: In Hebrew script r (ר) and d (ד) look almost the same, and copyists often confused them. Hadad was a common royal name in Edom (36:35; 1 Kings 11:14), so it is probably original, and several modern versions print it. The Plain English Translation keeps the reading of the Leningrad Codex, its base text, and lets the reader switch.
b: The same parallel list in 1 Chronicles 1:50 also calls his city Pai instead of Pau, another one-letter difference (י / ו).
